name: Static pods & etcd backup
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Maintenance & Troubleshooting. Drill EVERY node-level cluster-ops corner harder than the exam: static pods and mirror pods, repairing a crash-looping control-plane component, etcd snapshot backup, node taints and labels, cordon/drain for maintenance, uncordon to return a node, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly on persistent node/cluster state via docker exec and kubectl -o json.

questions.title: Static pod on a worker
questions.teach:
A **static pod** is run by the **kubelet** from a manifest in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on one node — the API server never schedules it. The API shows a read-only **mirror pod** named `<pod>-<node>`.

**Gotcha:** the manifest must live on the node you want the pod on — write it to `$W1`, or no mirror pod appears.
questions.prompt:
On worker node `$W1`, create a static pod named `static-web` (container `web`, image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) by writing a manifest into `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on that node.

Target: the mirror pod `static-web-$W1` is `Running` in namespace `default`, with image `busybox:1.36` and command `sleep 3600`.
questions.hint: In the exam you'd `ssh <node>`; in KindLab that's `docker exec -it $W1 bash`. Then `cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/` and create `static-web.yaml` — kind nodes have no vi, so use `cat > static-web.yaml <<'EOF' … EOF` — with a Pod named `static-web`. The kubelet forms the mirror pod `static-web-<node>` in ~15s.
questions.solution:
# 1) shell ONTO the worker node (exam equivalent: ssh <node>)
docker exec -it $W1 bash

# 2) now on the node: go to the static-pod dir and create the manifest (use vi in the exam)
cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
cat > static-web.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: static-web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF
exit

# 3) back on the base machine: verify the mirror pod
kubectl get pod static-web-$W1 -n default

verification.description: mirror pod static-web-$W1 Running with image busybox:1.36 + command sleep 3600

questions.eli5:
Normally when you want a pod, you ask the cluster boss (the API server) and the scheduler decides which node runs it. A **static pod** skips all that. It's like leaving a recipe card directly in a particular cook's drawer: the **kubelet** on one specific node watches a folder — `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` — and automatically cooks up any Pod manifest it finds there. No API server, no scheduler involved.

So to make a static pod called `static-web` on worker `$W1`, you shell onto `$W1` and drop a `static-web.yaml` manifest into that folder. Within about 15 seconds the kubelet starts it.

The API still *shows* you the pod, but what you see is a read-only photocopy called a **mirror pod**. Its name has the node name stapled on: `static-web-$W1`. You can look at it, but you can't edit or delete it through `kubectl` — the real control is the file on the node.

**Watch out:**

- **The manifest must be on the node you want the pod on.** Put it on `$W1`, or the mirror pod never appears. There's no "pick a node" field — the node *is* wherever the file lives.
- **The mirror pod is named `<pod>-<node>`**, e.g. `static-web-$W1`, not just `static-web`.
- **Don't try to `kubectl edit/delete` it** — it's read-only. Change or remove the file on the node instead; deleting the file removes the pod.
- **kind nodes have no `vi`** — create the file with a `cat > static-web.yaml <<'EOF' … EOF` heredoc.
- Only put a `name` in `metadata` (no namespace needed; mirror pods land in `default` unless the manifest says otherwise).
questions.deepDive:
## Static pods & mirror pods — full rundown

### Mental model
A **static pod** is managed directly by the **kubelet** on one node, not by the API server or scheduler. The kubelet watches its **static pod path** (default `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/`) and runs any Pod manifest it finds. The kubelet then creates a read-only **mirror pod** in the API so you can observe it — but you cannot control it through `kubectl`.

| | Normal pod | Static pod |
|---|---|---|
| Created by | you via API | kubelet from a file on the node |
| Scheduler involved | ✅ | ❌ |
| Where defined | etcd (via API) | `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/*.yaml` on the node |
| Pin to node | scheduler/affinity | by **which node's folder** the file is in |
| API object | the pod itself | **mirror pod** `<name>-<nodeName>` (read-only) |
| Edit/delete via kubectl | ✅ | ❌ (edit the file instead) |

The control-plane components (apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd) are themselves static pods on the control-plane node.

### Create one (on the node)
```bash
docker exec -it $W1 bash                 # exam: ssh <node>
cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/

# kind nodes have no vi/nano — use a heredoc
cat > static-web.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: static-web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF
exit

# back on base: the mirror pod appears in ~15s
kubectl get pod static-web-$W1 -n default -o wide
```

### How the kubelet reacts to the file
| File change | Kubelet action |
|---|---|
| Create manifest | starts the static pod + mirror pod (~15s) |
| Edit manifest | recreates the container(s) |
| **Delete** manifest | removes the static pod and its mirror pod |

### Finding/changing the static pod path
Set by the kubelet's `staticPodPath` (in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`) or the legacy `--pod-manifest-path` flag. kubeadm default: `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`.
```bash
grep staticPodPath /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Node selection = file location.** The pod runs on whichever node holds the manifest. Writing it to the wrong node → no mirror pod where you expected.
- **Mirror pod name is `<name>-<nodeName>`** — query that, not the bare `metadata.name`.
- **Don't `kubectl edit/delete` a static pod** — mirror pods are read-only. `kubectl delete pod static-web-$W1` just makes the kubelet recreate it; to truly remove it, delete the file on the node.
- **No editor on kind** — use `cat > … <<'EOF'`. Quote the heredoc marker (`'EOF'`) so `$` variables aren't expanded inside the manifest.
- A `namespace` in the manifest is honored; omit it and mirror pods appear in `default`.
- Keep YAML valid — a parse error means the kubelet silently won't create the pod; check `journalctl -u kubelet`.

### Quick reference
```bash
docker exec -it $W1 bash                              # ssh <node> in the exam
cat > /etc/kubernetes/manifests/static-web.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: static-web }
spec:
  containers:
  - { name: web, image: busybox:1.36, command: ["sleep","3600"] }
EOF
exit
kubectl get pod static-web-$W1 -n default              # mirror pod Running
# remove: delete the file on the node, NOT via kubectl
```

questions.title: Back up etcd
questions.teach:
**etcd** holds all cluster state; back it up with `etcdctl snapshot save`, authenticating via the certs under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/` against `https://127.0.0.1:2379`. Save into `/var/lib/etcd` (mounted on the node), then copy the file out.

**Gotcha:** the etcd image is **distroless — no shell**. Call `etcdctl` directly via `kubectl exec`; wrapping it in `sh -c '...'` fails.
questions.prompt:
Take an etcd snapshot and save it to `/opt/snapshot.db` on the control-plane node `$CP`.

Target: `/opt/snapshot.db` exists on `$CP` and is a real (>1KB) etcd snapshot.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-$CP -- etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db`, then `docker exec $CP cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db /opt/snapshot.db`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-"$CP" -- etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db
docker exec "$CP" cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db /opt/snapshot.db

verification.description: snapshot is a real (non-trivial, >1KB) etcd backup

questions.eli5:
**etcd** is the cluster's single notebook — it stores *everything* Kubernetes knows: every pod, secret, configmap, node, and setting. If etcd is lost, the cluster's memory is gone. So backing it up is one of the most important ops tasks, and it's a near-guaranteed exam question.

A backup is called a **snapshot**: a point-in-time photocopy of that notebook. You make one with the `etcdctl snapshot save` tool, writing the file somewhere on the control-plane node.

But etcd guards its notebook behind a locked door (TLS). To be let in, you must show three credentials: the certificate authority (`--cacert`), plus a client certificate and key (`--cert` / `--key`). On a kubeadm cluster these live under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/`. You also tell it where etcd listens: `--endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379`.

The trick: the easiest way to run `etcdctl` is *inside the etcd pod itself*, which already has the tool and the certs. So you `kubectl exec` into it, run the save to a folder that's mounted on the node (`/var/lib/etcd`), then copy the file out to its final home (`/opt/snapshot.db`).

**Watch out:**

- **The etcd image is distroless — it has NO shell.** You can't wrap the command in `sh -c '...'`; call `etcdctl` directly after `--`. `kubectl exec etcd-$CP -- etcdctl …`, not `-- sh -c "etcdctl …"`.
- **All three certs are required.** Missing one → `context deadline exceeded` or auth failure.
- **Write to a path visible on the node** (e.g. `/var/lib/etcd/...`) so you can copy it out, then `docker exec $CP cp` it to `/opt/snapshot.db`.
- A real snapshot is a **binary file well over 1KB**. If yours is tiny or looks like text, `etcdctl` didn't actually run — re-check your flags.
- If a question uses a newer tool, `etcdctl` may need `ETCDCTL_API=3` (v3.4+ defaults to 3).
questions.deepDive:
## Backing up etcd — full rundown

### Mental model
**etcd** is the key-value store holding **all** cluster state. A backup is a **snapshot** taken with `etcdctl snapshot save`, authenticated over TLS with the cluster's etcd certs. etcd is itself a static pod on the control-plane node (`etcd-<cp>` in `kube-system`), and its cert files live under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/`.

### The certs (kubeadm defaults)
| Flag | Default path | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `--cacert` | `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt` | CA that signed etcd's serving cert |
| `--cert` | `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt` | client cert |
| `--key` | `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key` | client key |
| `--endpoints` | `https://127.0.0.1:2379` | etcd listen address |

You can read the exact paths/endpoint from the etcd manifest:
```bash
grep -E 'listen-client-urls|cert-file|key-file|trusted-ca' \
  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
```

### Take the snapshot (from inside the etcd pod)
```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-$CP -- etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db

# copy it to the required location on the node
docker exec $CP cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db /opt/snapshot.db   # exam: already on the node
```
Write to `/var/lib/etcd` because that directory is mounted into the etcd pod **and** visible on the node, so you can retrieve the file.

### Verify / inspect a snapshot
```bash
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --write-out=table snapshot status /opt/snapshot.db
# shows hash, revision, total keys, size
```

### Restore (know the shape, even if not asked)
```bash
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /opt/snapshot.db \
  --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore
# then point etcd's static-pod manifest (hostPath volume) at the new data-dir and restart etcd
```
Restore creates a **new data dir**; you repoint etcd at it and restart — you don't restore in-place over a running etcd.

### etcdctl vs etcdutl
- `etcdctl snapshot save/status` — talks to a **running** etcd (needs endpoints + certs).
- `etcdutl snapshot restore` (newer etcd) — offline tool; restore no longer needs a running server. On older versions, `etcdctl snapshot restore` does it.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **etcd image is distroless — NO shell.** Call `etcdctl` directly after `--`; `kubectl exec etcd-$CP -- sh -c "etcdctl …"` **fails** (no `/bin/sh`).
- **All three TLS flags are mandatory.** Omit one → `context deadline exceeded`, `transport: authentication handshake failed`, or a hang.
- **`snapshot save` must run against ONE endpoint** — don't pass multiple comma-separated endpoints to save.
- Write the file to a **node-visible** path (`/var/lib/etcd/...`) so you can copy it out; writing only inside the container is useless.
- A genuine snapshot is a **binary bbolt DB, well over 1KB**. A tiny/text file means `etcdctl` never actually ran.
- v3.4+ defaults to API v3; on older tooling set `ETCDCTL_API=3` explicitly.
- Know the restore path flag is `--data-dir`, and that restore is **offline** + requires repointing etcd's manifest.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-$CP -- etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db
docker exec $CP cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db /opt/snapshot.db
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /opt/snapshot.db --write-out=table
```
